Module This chapter is part of the DP Module ("Dénombrement et Probabilités", that is, "Counting, Enumerating and Probabilities"). The prerequisites are: the LE Module ("Logic and Sets", seen during the seminar). Motivation « Counting » is a frequent activity for a computer scientist: counting the number of bits required to stock an integer number in a computer, counting the number of elementary operations required when executing an algorithm, counting the number of words of a given length that can be obtained from a finite alphabet, counting the number of connected or biconnected components in a graph, etc. This work is often related to the notion of « estimating » a number: indeed, it is sometimes difficult to get the exact number of realizations of the studied phenomenon, so we just try to find an upper or a lower bound, depending on our reason for counting. This estimation consists in getting the number of realizations in the best or worst case 1 . For example, when executing a brute force implementation to compute the Fibonacci sequence, it is difficult to predict the exact number of recursive calls. It is easier to get a lower and an upper bound for this number, both of them depending on the rank of the Fibonacci term we're computing. In the same way, when determining the GCD of two numbers, it is easier to get an upper bound for the number of Euclidean divisions that will be required, rather than getting this exact number. The latter is indeed very difficult to determine. Our purpose in the following is to bring you to a practical experience of counting . From a mathematical point of view, this work consists in enumerating ; the latter point refers to the lecture. It is a transversal activity. Answering the exercises will require you to employ many skills that you have developed in your past and new skills that we will develop now. These skills will be a great help for further activities, such as determining the complexity of algorithms or studying finite probability distributions. Learning outcomes As a general rule, we expect you to enumerate and count finite sets which can be handled by combinations, arrangements and permutations. The detailed learning outcomes are: • count the number of ways of picking elements from a finite set, with or without replacement, with or without repetitions; • count the number of mappings from a finite set to another; • adapt the typical methods to real life situations; • expand a binomial expression to a power n \in \mathbb{N} ; • prove the Pascal's formula, using either a counting or a computational method; • prove the binomial formula, using either a counting or a computational method; • imagine simple situations associated to a given way of counting. Some of these skills are transversal. Our main objective is that you engage in thinking and searching : considering hypotheses, testing them, finding counter examples. 1 It is hence different from a statistical estimation.

section: 1 Cardinal number of a finite set
content: 1 Cardinal number of a finite set 1.1 Summary Solving a counting problem consists in determining the number of elements in a given set. The first two sections rely on this point. The first section focuses on the behavior of the cardinal numbers 2 of sets when combined with the usual operations, while the second section deals with the modeling/formalization process: we will try to extract the main abstract ideas that may lead to the solution. This section is also the opportunity to apply some of the results about sets that we have seen before. Here, these concepts should be more tangible; it should be easier for you to try to feel your way toward the solution, using counter examples and building your own representations of sets and functions. You will note that, for some of the exercises, there are several ways to solve them. Typically, a direct method and a recursive method. It is important to understand the advantages and draw-backs of both ways of thinking 3 . On the one hand, the direct methods lead to explicit formulas, which directly provide all the information we're looking for (order of magnitude, comparisons). Yet they require a global understanding of the problem we are trying to solve. These methods are, hence, difficult to implement, but their results are easy to use. On the other hand, recursive methods provide the evolution of the result with the size of the problem, rather than the explicit result. If you really need the latter, you still have extra work to do in order to get an explicit formula. But implementing these methods requires only a local understanding of the problem, the underlying reasoning is more natural. Recursive methods are, hence, easier to implement, but their results are more difficult to use. In mathematics, we usually prefer an explicit formula which directly provides a numerical answer to a problem. It is not always true, however, when programming: a recursive formula can easily lead to a numerical answer, after entering into a loop which will quickly compute the successive intermediate values until the final one 4 . Many algorithmic tools (dynamic programming, memoization, etc.) enable this way of computing the final result. 1.2 Exercises Exercise 1.1 Let A (and B ) be the set of natural numbers which are multiples of 2 (and 3), smaller than or equal to 60. • What are the cardinal numbers of A and B ? • What can you say about the cardinal number of A \cap B ? • What is the cardinal number of A \times B ? The cardinal number of A \cup B ? Exercise 1.2 Let M and A denote the final grades in math and in algorithmics in S1 of EPITA. Both grades are between 0 and 20 and we suppose that they have integer values. Assuming that both modules have the same coefficient, a student tries to determine the number of combinations of A and M which may result in a global average equal to k \in \{1, \dots, 20\} . How can you help this student? You may, for example, represent the situation with a 2-entries table. Exercise 1.3 We focus on the cardinal number of the union of two sets A and B , whose intersection may be non-empty. 2 The most common ways to denote the cardinal number of a set A are: \text{Card}(A) , |A| , \#(A) etc. 3 The chapter about numerical sequences will raise this question again. 4 Paradoxically, you will see mathematical situations, such as the computation of a matrix determinant, where a recursive formula is more convenient than the explicit formula. Sometimes, the recursive method consists in a succession of easy to understand calculations, while the explicit formula is not tractable.

In computer science, it is frequent to think in terms of «class of problems»: if a problem can be reduced, that is, if it can be formulated as another well-known problem, then we say that both problems are equivalent and have the same underlying solution. That's why during class, we will work with abstract descriptions of the exercises: how do we connect the exercise to one of the reference problems? And how do we solve this reference problem? We will hence focus on the relation between the intuitive and the formal representations of different problems. 2.2 Exercises Exercise 2.7 1. A bag contains n balls, numbered from 1 to n . • We successively pick k balls from the bag, with replacement. How many possible ways of picking the balls? • We successively pick n balls from the bag, without replacement. How many possible ways of picking the balls? • We successively pick k balls from the bag, without replacement ( k \leq n ). How many possible ways of picking the balls? • We simultaneously pick k balls from the bag ( k \leq n ) and put them in another bag. How many possible results? 2. Let E be a n -element set and k \leq n . What is a k -element arrangement of E ? A permutation of E ? A k -element combination of E ? How many are there? Exercise 2.8 Find the numbers of • anagrams with the word computer • anagrams with the word mathematician • ways of calling 5 students from this class one by one to the blackboard. That is, the number of ways of choosing the 5 students and their order of call. • ways of calling all the students from this class one by one to the blackboard. • ways of calling all the students from this class one by one to the blackboard, given that the two students who came late this morning will be called twice. Exercise 2.9 A football club has a 24-player squad and the coach has to select the 11 players who will start the next match. Find the number of possible choices for the coach in the following situations: 1. Everyone in the squad can play at any position (goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, etc.). The coach just decides who plays, disregarding the positions of the players. 2. Everyone in the squad can play at any position. But the coach decides who plays and at which position. 3. Answer the previous questions if, from the squad, 3 players can only be goalkeepers while the 21 others can be at any position except goalkeeper.

Exercise 2.10 An association has 100 members. They have to select a 10-councilor board. Each councilor must be a member and the board will have: • A president • A treasurer • 8 other councilors No councilor can be at two positions simultaneously in the board. 1. How many possible boards are possible? 2. Answer the same question if, furthermore, the gender-parity is required. Assume the the members are 50 women, 50 men. If the president is a women, the treasurer must be a man and reversely. The other councilors must be 4 women, 4 men. Exercise 2.11 Let k and n be two non-zero natural numbers. For each of the following formulas, suggest a counting problem whose solution is the given formula 6 : • 2^n • \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} • k \cdot (n!) 3 Combinatorics 3.1 Summary Combinatorics deals with the different ways to rank finite sets or subsets: permutations, arrangements and combinations. These are often used as modeling processes for random experiments: picking cards, betting on the horses before a race and so on. It is natural then to apply these methods to finite probabilities: under the assumption of equiprobability of each possible result 7 , a finite probability question can be seen as a problem of getting the numbers of positive and possible results, the final probability being the ratio of these two numbers. These methods may also be applied to get an exhaustive enumeration of some sets: how many binary trees will fulfill a given property, or how many paths exist in a graph. Such enumerations can lead to an estimation of the complexity of some brute force algorithms (such as backtracking algorithms). 6 \binom{n}{k} can also be denoted by C_n^k (and not C_k^n ). You're expected to know both notations; they can be used in future works, MCQ, exams and so on. 7 When the results are not equiprobable, their enumeration and their relative frequencies enable the same reasoning.

3.2 Exercises ★ Exercise 3.12 This exercise is about the «permutations» of the set \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket , that is to say the bijections from this set into itself. 1. What is the total number of permutations of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket ? 2. Show that the composition of two permutations of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket is a permutation of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket . 3. Let f be a permutation of \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket . Show that there exist two distinct natural numbers p and q such that f^p = f^q . 4. Deduce that there exists a natural number r > 0 such that f^r = id_{\llbracket 1, n \rrbracket} . Exercise 3.13 The bookshelf of an EPITA student, reserved for «cramming» for the next exam, contains 4 algo books, 6 math books and 3 physics books. Determine the number of ways to rank them on the shelf, given that they must be classified according to the subject they refer to. Exercise 3.14 Let n \in \mathbb{N}^* and k \in \llbracket 0, n \rrbracket . 1. Compare the number of ways of choosing a subset of k elements from a set of n , with the number of ways of choosing a subset of n - k elements. Can you explain the resulting property? 2. In a box, there are n balls numbered 1 to n . We simultaneously pick k balls ( k \geq 1 ). (a) How many possible results are possible? (b) From these results, how many contain the 1-ball? Exercise 3.17 A candidate came to the Advance exam by bicycle. He locked his bike at the gate of the school, using a padlock with 4 digits (from 0 to 9). Then the math teacher asked him: 1. a. What is the number of possibilities for the padlock's code? b. What is the number of possibilities whose last digit is even? c. What is the number of possibilities which contain at least once the digit 2? 2. Suppose now that the code is made of 4 mutually distinct digits. a. What is the number of possibilities for the padlock's code? b. What is the number of possibilities whose last digit is even? c. What is the number of possibilities which contain at least once the digit 2? 4 In your programming activity 4.1 Summary Algorithmics and programming raise numerous counting problems. Here are some typical examples: • estimation of the number of iterations in a loop, or of how many times the loop will enter into a specified conditional instruction • estimation of the number of bits required to stock a natural number in memory • for a sorting algorithm, estimation of the input size, of the number of possible outputs, of the proportion of operations involving some specified sub-lists • words manipulation in language theory • estimation of the number of paths between two points in a graph. We suggest that you ask your algorithmics and programming teachers how these questions arise in their practical work. You may have been faced with some of them before; you will certainly be in the future. 4.2 Exercises Exercise 4.18 Let a and b be two natural numbers. 1. How many elements are there in \llbracket a, b \rrbracket ? 2. How many even elements in \llbracket 2, 10 \rrbracket and in \llbracket 2, 13 \rrbracket ? IGA vs AM The diagram illustrates the relationship between Identity Management (IGA) and Access Management (AM) across three phases: Before, During (runtime), and After. Identity Management (IGA) is associated with the Before phase. It involves managing identity, designing policies, approving access, and modeling roles. Authentication and Authorization are associated with the During (runtime) phase. This phase involves enforcing access decisions. Accounting is associated with the After phase. It involves reviewing logs, certifying access, and generating audit reports. Accounting is a cross-cutting concern that spans across all three phases. Practice Overview Goal: Understand separation of responsibilities The diagram illustrates the separation of responsibilities in an IAM system. It features three main components: MidPoint (IGA), Keycloak (AM), and an LDAP Directory, with an additional LDAP Admin UI. MidPoint (IGA) : Contains an Identity Store and Business Roles. It is associated with a PostgreSQL database. Keycloak (AM) : Contains Authentication, LDAP Federation, OIDC Tokens, and Session Management. It is also associated with a PostgreSQL database. LDAP Directory : A central directory containing User Accounts and Groups (admins, managers, users). LDAP Admin : A UI for LDAP management. Interactions are shown as follows: A large blue arrow labeled "LDAP Resource Provisioning" points from MidPoint (IGA) to the LDAP Directory. A blue arrow labeled "LDAP Federation" points from the LDAP Directory to Keycloak (AM). A small blue arrow points from the LDAP Directory to the LDAP Admin UI. Diagram illustrating the separation of responsibilities in an IAM system.

Knowledge-Based Authentication Methods Knowledge-based methods rely on ' something you know '. These are often the most familiar — but also the most vulnerable. Illustration of a password entry screen with the text 'Enter password' and a masked input field showing six asterisks. Case Study: RockYou2021 – Password Reuse Breach 1 Event In 2021, the largest known password leak occurred — called RockYou2021. 2 What Happened • Over 8 billion passwords were posted online in a mega leak. • Data was compiled from years of breaches (e.g., LinkedIn, Adobe). • Attackers used these for credential stuffing: trying passwords across many sites. 3 Why This Is a Knowledge-Based Failure Passwords = 'something you know' (knowledge factor). People reused the same passwords across services. No second factor (MFA) meant easy unauthorized access. 4 Lesson Passwords are easily leaked, guessed, or reused. Never rely on knowledge factors alone for secure authentication.

Case Study: Coinbase Breach via SIM-Swap (2022) A simple line-art icon of a calendar with a date marker. Calendar icon Event In 2022, attackers exploited SMS-based MFA to access Coinbase accounts. A simple line-art icon of two stylized human figures. People icon What Happened: Attackers used social engineering to perform a SIM-swap with the victim's mobile provider. Case: Samsung Galaxy S10 Fingerprint Bypass (2019) What Happened: 1 Galaxy S10 used an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor under the screen. With certain third-party screen protectors, any fingerprint could unlock the phone. The scanner misread patterns in the protector as valid fingerprints. Push-based Authentication graph LR; User[Login initiated by user] --> Server[Authentication server sends push notification]; Server --> Device[User approves or denies request]; Device --> Server; Server --> User; The diagram illustrates the Push-based Authentication process. It shows three main components: a user (represented by a computer icon), an authentication server (represented by a server rack icon), and a mobile device (represented by a smartphone icon). The process flow is as follows: 1. The user initiates a login. 2. The authentication server sends a push notification to the mobile device. 3. The user approves or denies the request on the mobile device. 4. The response is sent back to the server. 5. Finally, access is granted or blocked to the user. Diagram of the Push-based Authentication flow • Push authentication sends a login approval request to your mobile app. • You simply tap 'Approve' or 'Deny' on your device. • It requires real-time communication between the IAM system and your device. • Provides a smoother user experience compared to typing codes. • May include context like login location, device, or IP address. • Not supported natively in Keycloak; external services like Duo or Azure AD are used. Challenge-Response Authentication How It Works Used when the authenticator app requires the user to enter a code shown by the server. The server displays a numeric challenge (e.g., 849123). User Action User enters this challenge code into their authenticator app. Response Generation The app uses a shared secret to compute a one-time response. Authentication The server verifies this response to authenticate the user. This method is less common than TOTP but is useful for device pairing or extra security. sequenceDiagram

 Server-->>User: Send Challenge

The User sends a Respond to Challenge back to the Authentication Server . The Authentication Server sends a Pass / Deny response back to the User . Modern Passwordless Authentication: FIDO2 & Passkeys 1 FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online) and Passkeys represent the future of secure, passwordless login. 2 Key Concepts: - Passkey = a public/private key pair used to replace passwords - FIDO2 = the protocol standard behind passkeys - WebAuthn + CTAP (Client to Authenticator Protocol) - Platform Authenticators = built-in options like Windows Hello, Face ID 3 Benefits: - Phishing-resistant (no shared secrets) - Device-bound and origin-specific - Easy to use — login with fingerprint or face scan 4 Summary: Passwordless login is real and growing, powered by strong cryptography.  User->>Frontend: Initiate passkey creation
 Frontend->>Backend: Request credential data
 Backend-->>Frontend: Send user info, challenge, credential IDs, etc. Frontend->>Browser: navigator.credentials.create()
 Browser->>Passkey_provider: Generate passkey

 User-->>Passkey_provider: Successful verification

The process begins with the User initiating passkey creation, which is received by the Frontend. The Frontend then requests credential data from the Backend, which responds with user info, challenges, and credential IDs. The Frontend uses this to initiate navigator.credentials.create() in the Browser. The Browser generates a passkey and sends it to the Passkey provider for user verification. Upon successful verification, the Passkey provider creates the passkey and returns the public key to the Browser. The Browser then returns a public key credential to the Frontend, which sends it to the Backend. The Backend stores the public key and data, and finally sends a notification back to the User. Passkeys : Sign in Creating a passkey sequenceDiagram
 participant User
 participant PP as Passkey provider
 participant B as Browser
 participant F as Frontend
 participant BE as Backend

 User->>F: Visits sign-in page
 F->>BE: Request auth challenge
 BE-->>F: Respond with challenge
 F->>B: navigator.credentials.get()
 B->>PP: Show autofill passkey dialog
 PP-->>User: User verification
 User-->>PP: Successful verification
 PP-->>B: Return public key with signature
 B->>F: Resolve promise with credential (signature)
 F->>BE: Send public key credential (signature)
 BE->>BE: Verify against stored public key
 BE-->>F: Authentication success
 F-->>User: Sign-in success The diagram illustrates the sign-in process for passkeys. It involves five main components: User, Passkey provider, Browser, Frontend, and Backend. The process begins with the User visiting the sign-in page on the Frontend. The Frontend then requests an authentication challenge from the Backend. The Backend responds with the challenge, which the Frontend passes to the Browser via navigator.credentials.get() . The Browser shows an autofill passkey dialog to the User for verification. Upon successful verification, the Passkey provider returns a public key and a signature to the Browser. The Browser then resolves this promise and sends the credential (signature) to the Frontend. The Frontend sends the public key credential (signature) to the Backend, which verifies it against the stored public key. Once authentication is successful, the Frontend informs the User of sign-in success. From Method to Protocol: Why Protocols Matter Methods & Protocols Authentication methods = how users prove who they are (e.g., password, Face ID, smartcard). Authentication protocols = how systems communicate and validate that proof securely. 🧠 Analogy: 'Methods' are like saying your name; 'protocols' are the secure mail that delivers it to someone who needs to verify it. The Delivery Chain Think of protocols as the delivery mechanism that moves credentials between: • Your browser or app • An identity provider (like Google or Azure AD) • The system you're trying to access

They are set against a background of glowing circuit lines and data points. Why Authentication Protocols Matter ✓ Authentication protocols solve critical problems in digital identity: 1. Secure exchange of authentication data - Prevent replay or man-in-the-middle attacks 2. Interoperability across platforms and systems - Use Google login on a third-party app 3. Support federation (IDP ≠ Application) - Authenticate once, access multiple services 4. Enable method reuse (e.g., biometrics via FIDO2) - Consistent login across devices and channels 💡 Without protocols, authentication stays local and non-portable.

Common Authentication Protocols (Grouped by Context) Web SSO / Federation: OIDC: Modern protocol used for web logins (e.g., Google login). SAML: XML-based, used in enterprise apps (e.g., university portals). Network and Certificate-Based: RADIUS: Used in VPN and Wi-Fi authentication. X.509 / PKI: Certificate-based authentication (smartcards, email). Icon representing Web SSO / Federation Icon representing Internal / Legacy Systems Icon representing Network and Certificate-Based Icon representing Passwordless / Modern Internal / Legacy Systems: LDAP: Query protocol for identity directories (e.g., Active Directory). Kerberos: Ticket-based authentication in Windows environments. Passwordless / Modern: FIDO2: Public key cryptography for phishing-resistant authentication (e.g., YubiKey, Face ID).

Protocol Matching 1 VPN login → RADIUS - RADIUS is commonly used to authenticate remote access through VPNs. 2 Wi-Fi at school → Kerberos - Many school networks use Active Directory for authentication, which relies on Kerberos internally. - Especially relevant for domain-joined devices on Windows networks. 3 Google login on Trello → OIDC - This uses OpenID Connect for federated web login, authenticating via a third-party identity provider. Tip: Think about the environment — web, enterprise, or infrastructure — to match the right protocol.

SAML & OIDC as Authentication Protocols SAML and OIDC are protocols used to delegate authentication to a trusted Identity Provider (IdP). ✓ Purpose: • Allow users to log in once and access multiple applications (SSO). • Transfer identity information from IdP to applications. 🔄 Authentication Perspective: • User logs in at the Identity Provider. • IdP sends proof of identity to the application (e.g., via token or assertion). • The app trusts the IdP to verify the user. 1 We'll explore federation setups and deep-dive into these protocols in Session 5. SAML & OIDC as Authentication Protocols The diagram illustrates the SAML & OIDC authentication flow involving four main components: End User, Application (Client), Resource Provider (Relying Party), and Authorization Server. The flow is as follows: ① Authentication Request : The Application (Client) sends an authentication request to the Authorization Server. ② Access Token and ID Token : The Authorization Server returns the Access Token and ID Token to the Application (Client). ③ Resource Call : The Application (Client) calls the Resource Provider (Relying Party). ④ Access Token Validation : The Resource Provider (Relying Party) validates the Access Token with the Authorization Server. ⑤ Resource Response : The Resource Provider (Relying Party) returns the resource response to the Application (Client). SAML is common in enterprise environments with XML assertions. 2 Signing in with Google on a 3rd-party web app → OIDC. OIDC is ideal for modern web SSO using OAuth2 and JSON. 3 Legacy SaaS tool that only supports XML assertions → Many older applications were built with SAML-only support. 4 Mobile app that uses federated login → OIDC is lightweight and mobile-friendly, unlike SAML. Let's test your understanding of when to use SAML vs OIDC. 💬 Discuss with your neighbor: • What clues helped you decide? • Are both protocols still relevant today? → Be ready to share your logic! • 💡 Takeaway: SAML dominates older enterprise systems, while OIDC powers modern, web-based federation.

Access Control Model Definition An Access Control Model is a structured framework that defines how permissions are assigned and enforced to control access to digital resources. Mechanism Rather than assigning permissions directly to individual users, an access control model uses rules, roles, attributes, or policies to determine: • Who can access • What resources • Under what conditions

PBAC architectures 1 PEP – Policy Enforcement Point Intercepts user requests and enforces access decisions 2 PDP – Policy Decision Point Evaluates access requests against policies and returns allow/deny 3 PAP – Policy Administration Point The interface or tool where policies are created, managed, and stored 4 PIP – Policy Information Point Provides external attributes or context needed for decisions graph TD
 User((user)) -- "request access" --> PEP[PEP Enforce Policies]
 PEP --> Resource[Resource]
 PEP -- "can this user Access Resource?" --> PDP[PDP Evaluate Policies]
 PDP -- "YES/NO" --> PEP
 SecurityAdmin((Security Admin)) -- "create policy" --> PAP[PAP Manage Policies]
 PAP --> PDP
 PDP --> PIP[PIP Retrieve additional Attributes]
 PIP --> PDP
 PIP --- Context[Context: Org Chart, Cloud, DB] The diagram illustrates the PBAC architecture components and their interactions. A user requests access to a resource, which is intercepted by the PEP (Policy Enforcement Point). The PEP then asks the PDP (Policy Decision Point) if the user can access the resource. The PDP evaluates the request and returns a YES/NO decision to the PEP. The PEP then enforces the decision and either grants access to the resource or denies it. The PDP is also responsible for managing policies, which are created by the PAP (Policy Administration Point). The PAP is managed by a Security Admin. The PDP also interacts with the PIP (Policy Information Point) to retrieve additional attributes needed for decisions. The PIP is connected to various data sources, including an organization chart, a cloud, and a database. Diagram of PBAC architecture showing the flow between PEP, PDP, PAP, and PIP. Critical for Zero Trust and modern IAM

Additional Access Control Models 1 DAC – Discretionary Access Control Permissions are set by the resource owner. → Users decide who can access their files or resources. 2 MAC – Mandatory Access Control Permissions are based on system-enforced rules and classifications. → Users can't change access rights (common in military or government systems). 3 ReBAC – Relationship-Based Access Control Access is determined by the relationship between entities. → Example: A doctor can access a patient's records if assigned to them. 4 Context-Aware Access Control Access decisions include contextual factors. → Time, location, device type, risk score, etc.

What is Identity Lifecycle Management? Identity lifecycle management is the process of managing a digital identity from its creation to its eventual deactivation or deletion. It encompasses all the stages a user or system identity goes through during its existence within an organization. Identity lifecycle management involves provisioning (Joiner), modifying (Mover), and deprovisioning (Leaver) user accounts while ensuring secure and efficient access control throughout the lifecycle. Stages in Identity Lifecycle The identity lifecycle consists of three main stages that manage digital identities throughout their existence in an organization: Icon representing Provisioning: a shopping cart with a plus sign inside. Provisioning Definition: Creating and enabling user accounts to grant system access. Key Activities: • Create credentials and assign appropriate roles • Configure permissions based on job requirements • Allocate necessary resources and applications Example: New marketing employee receives access to design tools and relevant project files. Icon representing Modification: a document with a pencil and a left-pointing arrow. Modification Definition: Updating identity attributes and permissions as circumstances change. Triggers: • Promotions, transfers, or new responsibilities • Changes in policies or organizational structure Example: Sales rep promoted to manager gains access to team reports and budget systems. Icon representing Deprovisioning: a shield with a minus sign inside. Deprovisioning Definition: Disabling accounts and removing access when an identity is no longer active. Key Steps: • Deactivate accounts to prevent unauthorized access • Archive or transfer associated data as needed • Revoke access to all systems and resources Example: Departing employee loses access to email, CRM, and internal network.
The identity lifecycle consists of three main stages that manage digital identities throughout their existence in an organization:
• Create credentials and assign appropriate roles • Configure permissions based on job requirements • Allocate necessary resources and applications
• Deactivate accounts to prevent unauthorized access • Archive or transfer associated data as needed • Revoke access to all systems and resources

Onboarding Process (Joiner) The onboarding process is the first stage of the identity lifecycle. It involves creating and configuring user identities, assigning roles, and ensuring they have the resources needed to perform their tasks effectively. User Identity Creation • Create a unique user account in the identity management system. • Assign a username and configure initial credentials (e.g., password). Role Assignment • Assign the user to one or more roles based on their responsibilities. • Ensure roles align with the principle of least privilege, providing only the necessary access. Resource Allocation • Grant access to systems, applications, and tools required for their job. • Example: Email accounts, project management tools, file storage, etc. Communication of Policies • Share relevant company policies and security guidelines. • Example: Password management, acceptable use policies, and compliance requirements.

Offboarding Process The offboarding process ensures that when a user no longer requires access—due to resignation, termination, or role change—their accounts are securely deactivated, and their access to systems and data is removed to mitigate security risks. Account Deactivation Disable the user's accounts in the identity management system to block access immediately. Example: Deactivate email, network access, and application logins. Data Handling Archive or transfer ownership of files, emails, and other resources as necessary. Example: Reassign project files to a team lead. Access Revocation Icon representing access revocation, showing a document with a red 'X' mark. Remove access to all systems, including physical badges, VPNs, and cloud accounts. Example: Revoke access to project management tools, financial systems, and communication platforms. Compliance Checks Verify that all access rights have been revoked and ensure proper documentation.

The offboarding process ensures that when a user no longer requires access—due to resignation, termination, or role change—their accounts are securely deactivated, and their access to systems and data is removed to mitigate security risks.

Importance of a Secure Offboarding Process: Icon of a shield with a keyhole, representing access control. Prevents Unauthorized Access Eliminates risks of former employees or contractors accessing sensitive resources. Icon of a shield with a checkmark, representing security and protection. Ensures Data Security Protects company data by transferring or archiving user-owned files. Icon of a document with a checkmark, representing compliance and documentation. Aligns with Compliance Requirements Ensures the organization meets regulatory standards for identity and data management. Automating Offboarding: • Use identity lifecycle tools to trigger predefined workflows for account deactivation and data transfer. • Reduces errors and ensures consistency across offboarding procedures. Special Considerations for Offboarding Contractors: • Time-limited contracts require immediate offboarding upon contract expiration. • Systems should automatically deactivate access when the agreed-upon timeframe ends. Conclusion A secure offboarding process safeguards sensitive resources, reduces security risks, and ensures smooth transitions for teams and projects.

Challenges in Lifecycle Management Effectively managing the identity lifecycle can be complex, especially in dynamic and large-scale environments. Understanding these challenges helps organizations optimize workflows and enhance security. Handling Dynamic Identities Challenge: Managing users with changing roles, attributes, and responsibilities over time. Impact: Increased risk of misaligned access or unauthorized privileges. Solution: Automate identity updates using lifecycle management tools. Implement regular audits to align identities with current responsibilities. Reducing Errors in Manual Processes Challenge: Manual processes for provisioning, modifying, and deprovisioning identities are prone to human errors. Impact: Errors can lead to over-provisioning, security risks, or compliance violations. Solution: Leverage automation to streamline routine tasks and minimize human intervention. Use validation checks to detect and correct errors early. Ensuring Compliance with Policies Challenge: Meeting regulatory requirements and maintaining consistent enforcement of security policies. Impact: Non-compliance can lead to penalties, legal consequences, and reputational damage. Solution: Integrate governance tools to enforce policies and monitor access. Regularly update policies to reflect changes in regulations or organizational needs. Managing Role Creep Challenge: Users accumulate permissions over time, often retaining unnecessary privileges. Impact: Increases the risk of insider threats and unintentional misuse. Solution: Perform periodic access reviews to identify and revoke redundant permissions. Federated Identity – "Who you are and how your identity is trusted across domains" Federated Identity is a model of identity management where multiple distinct identity systems (e.g., from different organizations or domains) establish mutual trust to allow a user to authenticate in one domain and access resources in another without re-registering or managing separate credentials. Key Characteristics: • Based on trust relationships between Identity Providers (IdPs) and Service Providers (SPs). • The user's identity is managed by one domain but accepted by others. • Often uses standards like SAML, OIDC , or WS-Federation to transfer identity claims. • Identity Federation is the process of setting up and managing this trust. Examples: • Logging into a university library system using your university's central account. • An enterprise using Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) to access partner tools from another vendor.

Single Sign-On (SSO) – "How many times you have to authenticate" Definition: Single Sign-On is an authentication mechanism that allows a user to log in once and gain access to multiple applications or services without needing to log in again during the session. Key Characteristics: • SSO may operate within a single domain or across federated domains . • The goal is to minimize repeated login prompts while maintaining secure sessions. • Achieved through session tokens, cookies, or authentication assertions . • Commonly implemented using protocols like SAML, OIDC, Kerberos , etc.
Single Sign-On is an authentication mechanism that allows a user to log in once and gain access to multiple applications or services without needing to log in again during the session.

SAML Key Components of SAML: Assertions Data packets sent by the IdP to the SP to provide information about the user's identity and permissions. Types include Authentication Assertion, Attribute Assertion, and Authorization Decision Assertion. Identity Provider (IdP) Authenticates users and generates SAML assertions. Example: A corporate identity server or an external provider like Okta. Service Provider (SP) Receives the SAML assertion from the IdP and grants the user access to its services. Example: A web application or software service. SAML Advantages: 🔒 Centralized Authentication Users authenticate once with the IdP, streamlining the login process. ♥ Security Credentials are not shared with the SPs, reducing exposure to potential breaches. 📦 Scalability Supports seamless authentication across multiple SPs in enterprise environments.

OAuth2 Protocol The diagram illustrates the OAuth2 Protocol flow. A central user icon (a person with a thumbs up) is connected to four main components: the Client Application, the Resource Server, the Authorization Server, and the Resource Owner. The Client Application is shown as a laptop with a document icon. The Resource Server is shown as a server rack with a document icon. The Authorization Server is shown as a server rack with a document icon. The Resource Owner is shown as a server rack with a document icon. The flow is as follows: 1. The Client Application requests access from the Resource Owner. 2. The Resource Owner issues an access token to the Client Application. 3. The Client Application uses the access token to request access from the Resource Server. 4. The Resource Server grants access to the Client Application. 5. The Client Application also interacts with the Authorization Server, which verifies the user's identity and issues access tokens to the client application. Diagram of the OAuth2 Protocol flow OAuth2 - Delegated access OAuth2 is a token-based authorization protocol that enables secure access to resources on behalf of a user without exposing their credentials. Key Concepts of OAuth2: • Resource Owner: The user who owns the data or resources being accessed. • Client Application: The third-party application requesting access to the resource owner's data. • Authorization Server: Verifies the user's identity and issues access tokens to the client application. • Resource Server: Hosts the protected data or resources that the client application wants to access. Token types • Access Token: Used by the client application to access protected resources. • Refresh Token: Used to obtain a new access token without requiring user reauthentication. Advantages of OAuth2: Shield icon representing security Secure Authorization: User credentials are never exposed to client applications. OAuth2 is a token-based authorization protocol that enables secure access to resources on behalf of a user without exposing their credentials.

• Resource Owner: The user who owns the data or resources being accessed. • Client Application: The third-party application requesting access to the resource owner's data. • Authorization Server: Verifies the user's identity and issues access tokens to the client application. • Resource Server: Hosts the protected data or resources that the client application wants to access.
• Access Token: Used by the client application to access protected resources. • Refresh Token: Used to obtain a new access token without requiring user reauthentication.

How OAuth2 Supports Federation and Delegated Access OAuth2 is a token-based authorization protocol that enables secure access to resources on behalf of a user without exposing their credentials. Bob owns a vault at the bank. (1) Fran is a lawyer Bob wants to act on his behalf. (2) Bob contacts the Authorization Desk (Auth Server) and says: "Allow Fran to access my vault, but only to see documents, not withdraw cash." (3) The desk gives Fran an access slip (access token). Authorization Code Grant The diagram illustrates the Authorization Code Grant flow between four components: Resource Owner (Browser), Client App, Auth Server, and Resource Server. The flow is as follows: 1. The Resource Owner (Browser) clicks "Login". 2. The Client App redirects the Resource Owner (Browser) to the Auth Server. 3. The Resource Owner (Browser) is redirected to the Auth Server login page. 4. The Auth Server returns a login form to the Resource Owner (Browser). 5. The Resource Owner (Browser) enters their credentials and submits them to the Auth Server. 6. The Auth Server authenticates the user and redirects back to the Client App with an authorization code. 7. The Client App requests an access token from the Auth Server using the authorization code. 8. The Auth Server validates the code and returns an access token to the Client App. 9. The Client App makes an API request to the Resource Server using the access token. 10. The Resource Server validates the token and returns an API response to the Client App. 11. The Client App receives the API response from the Resource Server. Key events and data flows: Code: The authorization code is passed from the Auth Server to the Client App (Step 6). Access token: The access token is returned from the Auth Server to the Client App (Step 8) and used by the Client App to request data from the Resource Server (Step 9). How OpenID Connect Enables Federated Authentication Bob owns a vault at the bank. (1) Fran is a lawyer Bob wants to act on his behalf. (2) Bob contacts the Authorization Desk (Identity Provider) and says: "Authorize Fran to access my vault records, and issue a signed ID card to prove I approved this." (3) The Bank Access Desk ask Bob's Id (authentication). (4) After verification, the desk gives Fran an access slip (access token) and an Id Token proves Bob's identity and consent. (5) Fran goes to the Vault Clerk (Resource Server) and shows the slip (access token). Clerk checks: • Is this slip valid? • Is Fran allowed to view (not edit)? • Is it for Bob's vault? How OpenID Connect Enables SSO Bob owns 2 vaults at the bank. • Vault A: Financial records (used by Fran) • Vault B: Insurance policies (used by Alice) All vaults are managed by different Vault Clerks (Resource Servers). They all trust the same Bank Access Desk (Identity Provider). (1) Fran is a lawyer: "Can I access your financial vault? And prove it's really you who approved this?" Bob contacts the Authorization Desk (Identity Provider) and says: "Authorize Fran to access my vault A records, and issue a signed ID card to prove I approved this." The Bank Access Desk asks Bob's Id (authentication). After verification, the desk gives Fran an access slip (access token) and an Id Token proves Bob's identity and consent. (5) Fran goes to the Vault Clerk A (Resource Server A) and shows the slip. (6) Clerk checks the slip: If all pass → access granted ✅. So far, same steps as before (steps 2-4 are not shown anymore for clarity of the diagram) (7) Alice (Bob's insurance agent): "I need to see your insurance vault." (8) Bob is redirected again to the same Bank Access Desk (9) Since he is already authenticated, the Bank Access Desk immediately issues a new authorization code for Vault B. (10) – (11) Alice exchanges it and accesses Vault B — without Bob logging in again This is Single Sign-On — Bob logs in once, and that authentication is reused across multiple trusted services. Real-World Use Cases Federated identity and SSO are widely adopted in various domains, enhancing user experiences and streamlining access across systems. These technologies are integral to modern authentication and access management solutions. 1. Consumer Applications • Example: A user logs into services like Spotify, Airbnb, and Medium with their Google account. • Outcome: Simplifies user onboarding and improves retention by reducing barriers to access. 3. Government Services • Example: A citizen uses their government-issued digital ID to file taxes, renew a passport, and access healthcare services. (France Connect) • Outcome: Improves service delivery and simplifies interactions between citizens and government agencies. 5. E-Commerce and Payment Systems • Example: A shopper uses their PayPal account to log into various online stores and make payments. • Outcome: Improves customer satisfaction and fosters trust in e-commerce platforms. 2. Healthcare Systems • Example: A doctor logs into a hospital portal to view electronic health records (EHR) and access lab results using a single set of credentials. • Outcome: Enhances efficiency and ensures compliance with data protection regulations like HIPAA. 4. Educational Institutions • Example: A student logs into a university portal to access course materials, submit assignments, and register for classes. • Outcome: Enhances the educational experience and streamlines resource management for administrators.

Policies in IAM A policy in IAM is a formal statement that defines what should happen regarding identities, access, or security. It's a governance directive , not just a technical rule. Policy Type Example Enforced via Access Policy "Only HR staff can access payroll data" Role mappings, ABAC SoD Policy "No user can both approve and request expenses" SoD matrix Authentication Policy "MFA required for admins" IAM config (e.g., Keycloak) Account Policy "Inactive users are disabled after 90 days" Lifecycle workflows Logging & Audit Policy "All access must be logged and retained" SIEM*, IAM audit logs Approval Policy "High-risk roles need 2-level approval" IGA workflow engine *SIEM: Security Information and Event Management

Role Lifecycle Management 1. Role Mining ( Discovery ) Focus: Analyze existing access patterns Outcome: Identify logical groupings of permissions and candidate roles 2. Role Definition ( Design ) Focus: Define business-friendly role names and descriptions Outcome: Create structured RBAC models, assign appropriate permissions to each role 3. Role Assignment ( Deployment ) Focus: Map users or groups to roles Outcome: Operationalize access control 4. Role Review ( Governance ) Focus: Periodically evaluate roles: · Are they still needed? · Are permissions still appropriate? Outcome: Ensure roles stay valid & minimal

Role Definition: Designing Effective Access Roles Goal: Create clear, manageable roles that align with business functions. What to Define: • Role Name: Clear and business-readable (e.g., HR_Manager, Finance_Analyst) • Description: What is the purpose of this role? • Permissions: What resources and actions are included? • Scope: Is it department-wide, app-specific, or global? Types of Roles: • Business Roles: Align with job functions (e.g., Sales_Associate) • Technical Roles: Map to system permissions (e.g., DB_ReadOnly) • Composite Roles: Combine multiple roles into one (Keycloak supports this) Best Practices: • Use least privilege principle: no more access than needed • Avoid 'role explosion' (too many overly specific roles) • Reuse roles across systems if possible • Document everything clearly (owners, change process) Governance Tip: Roles should be reviewed and updated periodically to remain relevant and secure. What is Access Certification? Definition: Access Certification is a formal, recurring process where designated reviewers (e.g., managers or system owners) validate that users' access rights are appropriate and justified. Objective: Ensure that only authorized users retain access to systems and data Detect and remove outdated, excessive, or unauthorized access Meet regulatory and audit requirements (e.g., SOX, GDPR) Key Components: Review scope (users, systems, entitlements) Reviewers (managers, app owners, data owners) Attestation options (Approve, Revoke, Delegate) Justifications and comments Deadlines and escalation workflows Outcome: User System Access Reviewer Decision Justification Timestamp Alice HR System HR_Admin Bob Revoke No longer in HR 2025-06-03 10:15 AM Bob Finance Tool Viewer Clara Approve Needed for reporting 2025-06-03 10:18 AM Illustration of a woman in a business suit sitting at a desk, holding a tablet displaying a bar chart. Audit = Governance Process Audit refers to the systematic evaluation of IAM activities, controls, and compliance. It uses various data sources to determine: • Are access controls effective? • Are policies enforced? • Are users only accessing what they should? 1. Probability Space Probability theory is a branch of mathematics that studies the laws governing random phenomena, i.e. phenomena in which chance intervenes, such as a throw of a dice. In this chapter, we will describe the framework of probability and establish its terminology. We will not separate the presentation of the definitions from the role they play in modelling a concrete situation. A short history of probability 1 Today, probabilities are everywhere: they are at the heart of quantum physics, in the practical prediction of temporal processes (the stock market, the weather), in medical research, and so on. The term “probability” was first used in medieval jurisprudence. It comes from the Latin word “probare”, which means “to predict”. The calculation of probabilities was then an “art” whose aim was to determine the likelihood of an event. The development of probability as a mathematical science is therefore closely linked to games. The first problems were linked to games of dice and cards: the aim was to count the number of possibilities for a certain configuration to appear (e.g. the sum of two dice equals 7). But the problem that really launched the development of probability theory was the famous problem of points. 1 All the historical notes and remarks are mainly taken from the article Calcul des probabilités , Michel Loève, from the book Abrégé d'histoire des mathématiques 1700-1900 , under the direction of Jean Dieudonné, Tome II, Hermann, 1978.

Problem of points n players, each having initially bet a sum of money k , play a game of chance. The game stops when one of the players has won N rounds and the winner takes all the money bet nk . How should the prize be distributed if, for any reason whatsoever, the game is interrupted before the end? Some of the great Italian mathematicians of the 15th and 16th centuries (Pacioli, Cardano, Tartaglia), the same school that found the general solution to cubic equations and introduced complex numbers, tackled this problem but failed to provide a correct answer. The three founding fathers of the theory of probability are: ★ Blaise Pascal, French mathematician, who in 1654, in his correspondence with Pierre de Fermat, found the correct solution to the problem of points. The solution is closely related to Pascal's famous triangle, and uses the concept of probability of victory without actually saying so. ★ Christiaan Huygens, the great Dutch scientist of the 17th century, who in 1657 published De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae , the first work in which the concept of probability was rigorously stated and which recognised the importance of probabilities beyond games. 2 ★ Jacob Bernoulli, Swiss mathematician and physicist, who, in his posthumous work Ars Conjectandi of 1713, addresses the problem of a game of chance with two outcomes (win/loss) that is repeated identically n times (the famous Bernoulli experiment ). 1.1 Basic concepts Definition 1.1 (Random experiment, Sample space) A random experiment is a procedure whose outcome cannot be determined with certainty. The set of all possible outcomes is called the sample space , usually denoted by \Omega . Remark: By convention, all sample spaces are non empty, since we suppose that the random experiment under consideration has at least one possible outcome. Examples: i) When throwing a coin, \Omega = \{H, T\} where H means Heads and T means Tails. ii) When throwing a six-faced dice, the sample space is simply \Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} . The outcome of a throw is represented by the number of the face facing upwards. iii) When throwing two six-faced dice, the sample space is \Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}^2 . The outcome of this experiment is represented by the number shown in the first dice and the number shown in the second dice. iv) When measuring the lifetime of a smartphone (in days), one can decide to take \Omega = \mathbb{N} as the sample space. v) If we are at the bus stop and we know that the bus comes exactly every twelve minutes but we do not know when did the last bus come, our waiting time can be seen as a random experiment whose sample space is \Omega = [0, 12] . Definition 1.2 (Events) Given a random experiment, we call: ★ event , any subset of the sample space \Omega , ★ certain event , the event \Omega , ★ impossible event , the event \emptyset . Remark: This innocent-looking definition of events is problematic in the case of uncountable sample spaces, such as the one from the last example (the curious student can read section 1.4 to understand the subtleties of uncountable sample spaces). In this course, unless otherwise stated, we will always consider finite or countable sample spaces

These four operations can be seen from a logical point of view as logical connectives, but they can also be seen as describing occurrences of events of random experiments: Logical connectives Operations on sets Occurrence of events AND Intersection E \cap F the two events occur OR Union E \cup F at least one event occurs NOT Complement \bar{E} E does not occur \implies Subset E \subset F Each time that E occurs also F occurs Proposition 1.1 : Algebraic structure of set operations The basic operations on sets satisfy the following properties: 1. Commutativity of \cup and \cap : \forall (E, F) \subset \Omega^2, E \cup F = F \cup E \text{ and } E \cap F = F \cap E. 2. Associativity of \cup and \cap : \forall (E, F, G) \subset \Omega^3, (E \cup F) \cup G = E \cup (F \cup G) \text{ and } (E \cap F) \cap G = E \cap (F \cap G). 3. Idempotence of \cup and \cap : \forall E \subset \Omega, E \cup E = E = E \cap E. 4. \emptyset is the identity element of \cup and \Omega is the identity element of \cap : \forall E \subset \Omega, E \cup \emptyset = E = E \cap \Omega. 5. \Omega is the absorbing element of \cup and \emptyset is the absorbing element of \cap : \forall E \subset \Omega, E \cup \Omega = \Omega \text{ and } E \cap \emptyset = \emptyset. 6. Distributivity of \cup over \cap and of \cap over \cup : \forall (E, F, G) \subset \Omega^3, (E \cup F) \cap G = (E \cap G) \cup (F \cap G) \text{ and } (E \cap F) \cup G = (E \cup G) \cap (F \cup G).

We call this number the probability of the event. This is a real number with the interpretation that the greater the probability, the greater our confidence in the occurrence of the event. Intuitively, we identify the probability of an event with the asymptotic frequency with which that event occurs when the experiment is repeated infinitely often. So, by repeating an experiment N times, under the same conditions, and noting f_N(A) the frequency with which event A occurs, we take: P(A) = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} f_N(A) But this frequentist approach to probabilities has many problems, namely: ★ how do we know that the sequence f_N(A) converges? Definition 1.6 (Probability function) Let \Omega be a finite or countable set. Denote by \mathcal{P}(\Omega) the power set of \Omega (the set of all subsets). A probability function over \Omega is a function P : \mathcal{P}(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that: 1. \forall E \subset \Omega, 0 \leq P(E) \leq 1 . 2. P(\Omega) = 1 . 3. Additivity : for any sequence (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} of mutually incompatible events, we have P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i) The pair (\Omega, P) is called a probability space , and for any event E \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega) , the number P(E) \in [0, 1] is called the probability of E . ◆ Examples: i) Uniform probability 4 : Let \Omega be a finite set, E \subset \Omega an event and define P : \mathcal{P}(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R} by P(E) = \frac{\text{card}(E)}{\text{card}(\Omega)} \quad (\text{"favourable outcomes over possible outcomes"}) Then P is a probability function over \Omega , called uniform over \Omega since all elementary events have equal probability. This uniform probability shows up in many situations and, in this case, the computation of probabilities is reduced to a computation of cardinalities. ii) Let \Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots\} be a finite or countable sample space. Then, any function p : \Omega \rightarrow [0, 1] such that \sum_{\Omega} p(\omega_i) = 1 can be used to define a probability function over \Omega through \forall E \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega), P(E) = \sum_{x \in E} p(x). In other words, any probability function is completely determined by a sequence of positive real numbers whose sum equals 1. 4 This example makes the link between the abstract axiomatic approach and the intuition of what probabilities are.

Proposition 1.3 Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space. Then: * P(\emptyset) = 0 , * P(\bar{E}) = 1 - P(E) , * E \subset F \implies P(E) \leq P(F) , * P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F) - P(E \cap F) . Proof. First of all, you only need to look again at the drawings of operations on sets and think of probability as the relative surface of a subset to get an intuitive understanding of these results. Formally (this is a good exercise to familiarise yourself with the properties of probability functions) * We have \emptyset \cap \Omega = \emptyset and \emptyset \cup \Omega = \Omega therefore P(\emptyset \cup \Omega) = P(\emptyset) + P(\Omega) = P(\Omega) . This yields P(\emptyset) = 0 . * Since E \cap \bar{E} = \emptyset , we have P(E \cup \bar{E}) = P(E) + P(\bar{E}) . Moreover, we have E \cup \bar{E} = \Omega . This yields P(E) + P(\bar{E}) = P(\Omega) = 1 . * If E \subset F , we have F = E \cup (F \cap \bar{E}) . Moreover, since E \cap (F \cap \bar{E}) = \emptyset , we have P(F) = P(E) + P(F \cap \bar{E}) . Finally, since P(F \cap \bar{E}) \geq 0 , we have P(F) \geq P(E) . * We have E \cup F = E \cup (F \cap \bar{E}) . Since E \cap (F \cap \bar{E}) = \emptyset , we have P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F \cap \bar{E}) . Moreover, F = (E \cap F) \cup (F \cap \bar{E}) and these last two events are incompatible. Thus P(F) = P(E \cap F) + P(F \cap \bar{E}) and we conclude that P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F) - P(E \cap F) . \square Proposition 1.4 : Inclusion-Exclusion principle (Poincaré's formula) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space \{E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n\} any family of events. We have: P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i\right) = \sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k+1} \sum_{1 \leq i_1 < \dots < i_k \leq n} P(E_{i_1} \cap \dots \cap E_{i_k}) \\ = \sum_{i=1}^n P(E_i) - \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} P(E_i \cap E_j) + \sum_{1 \leq i < j < k \leq n} P(E_i \cap E_j \cap E_k) + \dots + (-1)^{n+1} P\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n E_i\right).

Let us then start by defining these Vitali sets: Let \mathcal{B} be the set of all real numbers belonging to the interval [0, 1[ whose binary writing is finite. Moreover, let us define on [0, 1] the following equivalence relation \begin{aligned} x \sim y &\iff \exists b \in \mathcal{B}, x = y \oplus b \\ &\iff \begin{array}{l} \text{one can switch from the binary writing of } x \text{ to that} \\ \text{of } y \text{ with a finite number of modifications.} \end{array} \end{aligned} For example, one has 15/100 = 0.00100110011001100110011\dots \text{ and } 65/100 = 0.10100110011001100110011\dots, therefore 15/100 \sim 65/100 since their binary writings differ only in the first digit. Suppose we possess an infinitely large urn, an infinite collection of balls numbered 1,2,3,... and consider the following though experiment: ★ one minute before midnight, balls 1 through 10 are placed in the urn and ball 10 is withdrawn. ★ 1/2 minute before midnight, balls 11 through 20 are placed in the urn and ball 20 is withdrawn. ★ 1/4 minute before midnight, balls 21 through 30 are placed in the urn and ball 30 is withdrawn. ★ 1/8 minute before midnight, balls 31 through 40 are placed in the urn and ball 40 is withdrawn. ★ etc ... a) For n \in \mathbb{N}^* , what is the probability that a ball is withdrawn at some moment before midnight? Conditional probabilities In practical computations of probabilities, we are quickly confronted with two types of situation which lead us to introduce the concept of "conditional probability": ★ Firstly, there are situations where we have partial information about the outcome of the random experiment, information that must be taken into account because it often modifies the probabilities of the outcome. The probability that a person is under 20 years of age is not the same if we also know that this person is a student at EFREI or that he or she is capable of proving the central limit theorem. ★ Then, even when partial information is not known, it is often easier to calculate the probability we want by making a distinction between cases: if we want to calculate the probability that a citizen of the European Union will vote for the Green party in the next European elections, the easiest way is to look at what happens country by country (probability knowing that he or she is French, German, Hungarian, etc).

2.1 Definition and basic properties Definition 2.1 (Conditional probability) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space and let E, F be two events of \Omega such that F is not impossible. Then, the probability of E knowing F (or conditional probability of E on F ), denoted P(E|F) or P_F(E) , is defined by: P_F(E) = P(E|F) = \frac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)}. This definition should be easy to understand: everything happens as if F had occurred, so we're only looking at the set F which “replaces” the sample space \Omega . The intersection of E and F is shaded blue. The right diagram shows the same sample space Omega, but with a hatched background, indicating that the sample space is now restricted to F. The intersection of E and F is still shaded blue, but the area of E that does not overlap with F is now hatched, indicating it is ignored. An arrow labeled 'Condition on F' points from the left diagram to the right diagram. Figure 2.1 – The probability of occurrence of event E is the ratio of the blue surface over the surface of the whole sample space (grey area). When conditioning on F (right figure), the sample space becomes smaller and the hatched area is ignored. ◆ Example: Consider the following experiment: we draw, successively and without replacement, two balls from an urn that contains initially two black balls and two white balls. Then, we have \begin{aligned} P(E_1 \cap E_2) &= P(E_2|E_1)P(E_1), \\ P(E_1 \cap E_2 \cap E_3) &= P(E_3|E_1 \cap E_2)P(E_2|E_1)P(E_1) \end{aligned} and, more generally, P\left(\bigcap_{1 \leq i \leq n} E_i\right) = P\left(E_n \mid \bigcap_{1 \leq i \leq n-1} E_i\right) P\left(E_{n-1} \mid \bigcap_{1 \leq i \leq n-2} E_i\right) \cdots P(E_2|E_1)P(E_1). Proposition 2.4 Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space and E and F two events. We have E \text{ and } F \text{ independent} \iff E \text{ and } \bar{F} \text{ independent.} Proof. See exercise 2.3. □ For families of more than two events, you might expect it to be sufficient to check that all pairs of events are independent. But the following example shows that this is not the case. ♦ Example: Throw two fair dices and consider the following events: E = the sum equals 7, F = the first dice yields 4, G = the second dice yields 3. We have P(E|F) = P(E|G) = P(F|G) = P(E) = P(F) = \frac{1}{6} therefore (E, F) , (E, G) and (F, G) are the pairs of independent events. But clearly E and F \cap G are not independent since P(E|F \cap G) = 1 . 2.2 Bayes' formula The purpose of Bayes' formula is to allow us to go from P(E|A) to P(A|E) . There are many situations where this problem is of great interest. Let us take a simple example from statistics in medicine, where there are enough patients with a certain pathology coming into a department. We receive sick patients and we can easily calculate the proportion who have been vaccinated, for example. So we have two events: sick S and vaccinated V . This count gives us the proportion of vaccinated patients among the incoming patients, i.e. the probability P(V|S) . But what we are interested in is the probability of falling ill knowing that you have been vaccinated, i.e. P(S|V) 1 . Theorem 2.6 : Bayes' theorem Let \mathcal{A} = \{A_1, \dots, A_n\} be a partition of \Omega and E be any event. Then, we have P(A_j|E) = \frac{P(E|A_j)P(A_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(E|A_i)P(A_i)}. Proof. It suffices to combine the total probability formula and the definition of conditional probabilities to obtain Bayes' theorem. Indeed: P(A_j|E) = \frac{P(A_j \cap E)}{P(E)} = \frac{P(E|A_j)P(A_j)}{P(E)} = \frac{P(E|A_j)P(A_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(E|A_i)P(A_i)}. □ Remark: Often, events A_j are thought of as “hypotheses” and in this case Bayes' formula shows us how to modify our opinions about these hypotheses when an event E occurs (see 2.3 for more details on this point of view on probability as a confidence measure). ♦ Example: A doctor is called in to see a sick child. The doctor has prior information that 90% of the sick children in this neighbourhood have influenza, while the remaining 10% have measles. For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that there are no other illnesses in this neighbourhood. A well-known symptom of measles is a rash. Let's assume that the probability of getting a rash if you have measles is 0.95. However, sometimes children with flu also develop a rash, and the probability of having a rash if you have flu is 0.1. On examining the child, the doctor finds a rash. What is the likelihood of the child having measles? On pose les events G = “to have the flu” R = “to have measles” EC = “to develop a rash” We want to compute P(R|EC) . The events G and R constitute a partition and, according to Bayes' theorem, we have: P(R|EC) = \frac{P(EC|R)P(R)}{P(EC|R)P(R) + P(EC|G)P(G)} = \frac{0.95 \times 0.1}{0.95 \times 0.1 + 0.1 \times 0.9} \approx 0.51. So the child has almost as much chance of having measles as flu!

Historical Note #1 (Thomas Bayes and “his” formula) Thomas Bayes (1701-1761) was a British mathematician who was destined for oblivion: his work on probability was published in 1761 after his death and found very few readers. But his formula was rediscovered in 1774 by the brilliant young French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace. It was Laplace who gave it the name "Bayes' Theorem" in 1781 after a visit from Richard Price, a friend of Bayes, who told him about the British mathematician's work. What's more, Laplace placed Bayes' formula at the centre of a new interpretation of probability, known today as Bayesian, even though there is no evidence that Thomas Bayes himself subscribed to this interpretation. 2.3 (Hors programme) : un peu de philosophie Probability is the most important concept in modern science, especially as nobody has the slightest notion what it means Bertrand Russell After the work of Andreï Kolmogorov in the 1930s, a mathematician has no doubts about what a probability is: he will simply take the abstract definition 1.6, page 15 (or more exactly the even more abstract definition 1.9, page 23). But, as soon as we leave the strict confines of mathematics - and it is precisely outside mathematics that probability acquires its importance - the precise meaning of the concept of "probability" is much more elusive than we might naively believe. Statements such as "the probability that I will roll a six on the next throw of the dice is 1/6 " or "the probability that this carbon-14 atom will decay in the next 5734 years is 0.5" are taken as objective descriptions of a certain reality in the world. Here, their interpretation seems clear enough: for example, the first statement says that, if I repeated the throw of the dice 600 times, I would land on 6 approximately one hundred times and that if I made an infinite number of throws, the proportion of times I would land on 6 would be exactly one sixth. This interpretation of probabilities is known as the frequency interpretation: Frequency interpretation of probabilities The probability of event E is understood as the relative frequency of occurrence of event E in a infinitely long run of repetitions of the random experiment. This interpretation was implicit in De Moivre, Poisson and Gauss and was defined explicitly by Mills, Ellis, Cournot and Fries. It was the dominant view in science until the beginning of the twentieth century and continues to be so in common discussion today. But, apart from the obvious problems associated with the appearance of infinity in this definition 2 , the frequency interpretation becomes more problematic for statements like "the probability of rain tomorrow is 80%" or, even worse, "the probability of Carlos Alcaraz winning the next US Open tennis tournament is 30%". The main problem is clearly that the experiments in question cannot be repeated. But an even deeper problem is that we can question the objective nature of the preceding assertions and see them as assertions about the subjective knowledge and beliefs of the person proclaiming them. 2 Take a counter-intuitive probability result, for example the one in exercise 1.13, and try to convince your non-scientific friends who are reluctant to accept the result by experiment. You will see that, very often, the experiment will prove you wrong, to which you will retort, somewhat embarrassed: "If we had repeated the experiment more times, you would have seen that the result is true". To give an easy, concrete example: the probability that, out of 10,000 throws of a coin, there are exactly 5,000 heads and 5,000 tails is only 0.008!

Bayesian or subjective interpretation of probabilities The probability of event E is a measure of the subjective belief that a person has in the future occurrence of event E given her current state of knowledge. According to this view, the claim “the probability that the dice will yield a six in the next throw is 1/6 ” shows, in fact, that one has no knowledge about the precise speed and angular momentum of the dice when it will leave the hand of the person throwing the dice and about the details of how fair the dice is. Therefore, in Bayesianism, probabilities are always conditional probabilities (there is no meaning to what an absolute probability could be) and Bayes’ theorem describes precisely the process of learning: the formula shows how the beliefs (of a rational agent) on information A_j evolve as we discover the existence of certain events E . This second approach to the meaning of probabilities turned out to be very productive in statistics since it motivated a whole branch of the field called Bayesian inference. At the end of the year, market share changes as follows: ★ The customers of company A split equally between A , B and C the following year. ★ Customers of company B always remain loyal to this company. ★ The customers of the company C will be the following year customers of A with a probability \frac{1}{12} , of B with a probability \frac{7}{12} and of C with a probability \frac{1}{3} . For n \in \mathbb{N} , a_n , b_n and c_n are the probabilities that, at the end of the n -th year, a consumer will decide to subscribe to A , B or C the following year. a) Determine a recursion relationship between a_n , b_n , c_n and a_{n+1} , b_{n+1} , c_{n+1} . b) Deduce the expression of a_n , b_n and c_n as a function of n . Constant-recursive sequences of order 2 will appear and we will use the following flashcard method . c) Determine the limit of these sequences. Is there an operator which tends towards a monopoly position? Flashcard method: Let (u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} be a sequence satisfying: \forall n \in \mathbb{N} , u_{n+2} + au_{n+1} + bu_n = 0 , where a, b \in \mathbb{R} are two constants. To find the expression of u_n as a function of n , we use the method of the characteristic equation: i. Consider the characteristic equation X^2 + aX + b = 0 and compute its roots q_1 and q_2 (which might eventually be the same). ii. ★ If q_1 \neq q_2 , we have \forall n \in \mathbb{N} , u_n = \alpha \cdot q_1^n + \beta \cdot q_2^n with \alpha and \beta two constants. ★ If q_1 = q_2 = q , we have \forall n \in \mathbb{N} , u_n = (\alpha \cdot n + \beta) \cdot q^n with \alpha and \beta two constants. iii. The constants \alpha and \beta are found using the data of the problem. More often than not, u_0 and u_1 are known and this yields a linear system of two equations to solve for \alpha and \beta . 3. Discrete Random Variables Often, when dealing with random experiments, we are not really interested in the outcome but rather in a certain quantity related to the outcome. For instance, we can ★ randomly pick a person amongst the french population and measure her height or the average number of sleeping hours per day, ★ randomly pick a third year EFREI student and measure his/her grade in last year's probability final exam, ★ throw two dice and compute the sum of the outcomes. These values that we build out of the outcomes of random experiments are called “random variables” and studying their properties constitutes the heart of probability theory. 3.1 Basic definitions Definition 3.1 (Random variable) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space. A random variable is simply a function X : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} . The set of all possible values of X is called the range of X and is denoted X(\Omega) . The set of all random variables over \Omega is denoted \mathbb{R}^\Omega . Examples: Continuing with the examples of the introduction:

★ If \Omega = \{\text{french population}\} and P is the uniform probability over \Omega , then height and average sleeping hours per day are two functions H, S : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} whose supports are, respectively, [25, 222] (in cm) and [3, 18] (in hours). ★ If \Omega = \{\text{third year EFREI students}\} and P is the uniform probability over \Omega , then the grade of last year's final exam is a function G : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} whose range is the interval [0, 20] . ★ When throwing a pair of dice, \Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}^2 and the sum of the outcomes is a function S : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} whose range is \{2, 3, 4, \dots, 12\} . Definition 3.2 (Operations on random variables) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space, X, Y two random variables and \lambda \in \mathbb{R} . Then: 1. \mathbb{R}^\Omega is a real vector space. In other words, X + Y and \lambda.X are random variables. 2. The product X.Y is also a random variable. 3. Let f be a real-valued function defined over X(\Omega) , then the composition f(X) defined by \Omega \xrightarrow{X} \mathbb{R} \xrightarrow{f} \mathbb{R} is also a random variable. Examples: ★ For the third year EFREI students, denote by X the grade at last year's final exam of the probability course and Y the grade at last year's mid term exam. Then Z = 0.6X + 0.4Y is a random variable (it is the final grade of the probability course). ★ For the French population, let H be the height of a person, M his/her weight and f the function defined by f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2} . Then, IMC = P \times f(H) = \frac{P}{H^2} is a random variable (it is the body mass index). Definition 3.3 (Discrete random variable) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space and X a random variable. A random variable X is discrete whenever the range X(\Omega) is finite or countable. The set of discrete random variables \Omega is denoted \ell(\Omega) . Examples: ★ The random variable X = \text{"grade at last year's probability final exam"} can be seen as either discrete or not depending on our model. If one considers that the grade can in principle be any real number in the interval [0, 20] , then X fails to be discrete. But a more realistic model is to consider that grades are defined up to a half-point, in which case the range is X(\Omega) = \{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, \dots, 19, 19.5, 20\} and therefore X is discrete.
